subject: food dropped on floor
title: What If the 5-Second Rule Were Real?

scenes.text: What if the five-second rule were true? Scientists tested it 2,560 times.
At Rutgers, researchers coated steel, tile, wood and carpet with bacteria, then dropped food on them.
Watermelon, bread, buttered bread and gummy candy, left for under a second, five, thirty, or three hundred seconds.
Bacteria jumped onto the food in under one second. Longer meant more, but no moment was safe.
Wet food was worst. Watermelon picked up the most. Gummy candy, the least.
The real surprise: carpet passed on the fewest bacteria. The rule is a myth, and the rug beats the tile.

description:
A 2016 Rutgers study (Applied and Environmental Microbiology) tested four foods on four surfaces at four contact times, 2,560 measurements in all, using a harmless relative of Salmonella.
Transfer sometimes began in under a second; watermelon picked up the most, gummy candy the least, and carpet transferred far less than tile or steel.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Be honest: what's the longest you've left food on the floor and still eaten it?
